provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Comprehension: leadership and service
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to read and answer questions on leadership and service passages, make inferences from the text, and identify main ideas.

Introduction:
We have practiced reading comprehension before. Today we will read passages about leadership and service in Nigeria.

Content:
Leadership means guiding people like a headmaster in a school or a governor in a state. Service means helping others like when market traders give extra food to poor customers. When we read, we look for what is directly stated and what we can infer. For example, if a passage says "The chairman worked from morning till night", we can infer that he is hardworking.

Class activity:
In pairs, read a passage about a Nigerian community leader who built a well. Answer questions and discuss what his actions show about his character.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is leadership?
2. Give an example of service in your community.
3. What can you infer from "The teacher marked books until his hands hurt"?
4. Why is service important in Nigeria?

Summary:
Good leaders serve others and we can understand passages better by looking at both what is stated and what we can infer.

topics.title: Grammar: question tags
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to form question tags correctly, use them in sentences, and practice them in dialogues.

Introduction:
We use questions to get information. Today we will learn question tags which are short questions at the end of sentences.

Content:
A question tag is a small question added to a statement. If the statement is positive, the tag is negative, and vice versa. For example: "You are coming to the party, aren't you?" When the main verb is "am", the tag is "aren't I?". For "can", we use "can't you?", like "You can swim, can't you?". In Nigeria, we use question tags when talking with friends or elders to show we are paying attention.

Class activity:
Work in pairs. Create dialogues using question tags about everyday activities like going to the market or attending a wedding.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is a question tag?
2. Add the correct question tag: "It is raining, ______?"
3. Change this statement to a question tag: "You like jollof rice."
4. When would you use a question tag in a conversation?

Summary:
Question tags help us confirm information and make our conversations more engaging in Nigerian English.

topics.title: Grammar: phrasal verbs
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify common phrasal verbs, use them correctly in sentences, and practice them in fill-in exercises.

Introduction:
We have learned single verbs like "go" and "come". Today we will learn phrasal verbs which are verbs plus small words that change the meaning.

Content:
A phrasal verb is a verb plus a preposition or adverb that creates a new meaning. For example, "look after" means to take care of, like when you look after your younger siblings. "Turn on" means to start something electrical, like turning on the generator during NEPA outage. "Give up" means to stop trying, like when students give up on difficult math problems. In Nigerian English, we use phrasal verbs every day when talking about household chores or daily activities.

Class activity:
Complete sentences with the correct phrasal verbs from a list. Then create your own sentences using these phrasal verbs about Nigerian life.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is a phrasal verb?
2. What does "look after" mean?
3. Use "turn on" in a sentence about electricity in Nigeria.
4. Why are phrasal verbs important in English?

Summary:
Phrasal verbs are common in everyday English and help us express ideas more precisely in conversations and writing.

topics.title: Vocabulary: prefixes and suffixes
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify prefixes and suffixes, use them to form new words, and guess meanings of unfamiliar words.

Introduction:
We know many English words. Today we will learn how to build new words using prefixes and suffixes.

Content:
A prefix is a letter or group of letters added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning. For example, "un-" in "unhappy" means not. "Mis-" in "misunderstand" means wrong. A suffix is added to the end of a word. "-ful" in "helpful" means full of. "-less" in "careless" means without. In Nigerian markets, traders use words like "overripe" or ``underripe`` to describe fruits, using prefixes to show condition.

Class activity:
In groups, take base words like ``care`` or ``kind`` and add different prefixes and suffixes to form as many new words as possible.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is a prefix? Give an example.
2. What does the suffix ``-less`` mean?
3. Add a prefix to ``happy`` to make its opposite.
4. How can prefixes and suffixes help you understand new words?

Summary:
Prefixes and suffixes are powerful tools for building vocabulary and understanding unfamiliar words in English.

topics.title: Composition: expository essay
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to plan an expository essay, write about drug abuse dangers, and organize their ideas clearly.

Introduction:
We have written different types of essays. Today we will learn to write expository essays that explain a topic clearly.

Content:
An expository essay explains a topic without personal opinions. To write about drug abuse dangers, first plan your ideas: introduction, causes, effects, solutions. In the introduction, define drug abuse and why it matters. In causes, mention peer pressure and curiosity. In effects, discuss health problems like liver damage and social issues like theft. In solutions, suggest education and community programs. Use Nigerian examples like the dangers of codeine cough syrup abuse among youth.

Class activity:
Create an outline for an expository essay on drug abuse dangers. Then write the full essay using your outline.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is an expository essay?
2. List three dangers of drug abuse.
3. What should be included in the introduction of this essay?
4. How would you organize the causes of drug abuse?

Summary:
Expository essays explain topics clearly with facts and examples, making them useful for discussing important issues like drug abuse in Nigeria.

topics.title: Formal letter
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify the format of a formal letter, write a letter of application correctly, and use appropriate language.

Introduction:
We write letters to communicate with people we don't know well. Today we will learn formal letters, especially letters of application.

Content:
A formal letter has a specific format: your address at the top right, then the date, recipient's address on left, salutation like "Dear Sir/Madam", then body paragraphs, and closing like "Yours faithfully". A letter of application is when you apply for something like a school or job. In the first paragraph, state what you are applying for. In middle paragraphs, explain your qualifications and experience. In the final paragraph, express willingness to attend an interview. Use formal language and avoid slang. For example, when applying for a scholarship, mention your good grades and extracurricular activities.

Class activity:
Write a letter of application for a fictional scholarship to a Nigerian secondary school, following the proper format.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are the main parts of a formal letter?
2. How do you start a formal letter to someone whose name you don't know?
3. What should you include in the body of an application letter?
4. Why is formal language important in these letters?

Summary:
Formal letters follow a specific format and use appropriate language to communicate professionally in situations like job or school applications.

topics.title: Oral: vowel contrasts
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between vowel sounds, pronounce minimal pairs correctly, and listen to identify vowel contrasts.

Introduction:
English has different vowel sounds that can change word meanings. Today we will practice contrasting these sounds.

Content:
Vowel contrasts are different vowel sounds that can change word meanings. Minimal pairs are words that differ by only one sound. For example, ``ship`` and ``sheep`` contrast in the vowel sound. In Nigerian English, some vowel contrasts can be challenging, like ``bat`` and ``bet``. Practice by placing your tongue differently: for ``see`` your mouth is wide, for ``sit`` it is more relaxed. During Harmattan season, people might say ``cold`` instead of ``called`` if they don't distinguish these vowels clearly.

Class activity:
Work in pairs. Practice minimal pairs like ``live`` and ``leave``, ``full`` and ``fool``. Listen and repeat after the teacher, then create sentences using each word.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are minimal pairs?
2. Give an example of vowel contrast in English.
3. How does your mouth position change between ``see`` and ``sit``?
4. Why is practicing vowel contrasts important for clear speech?

Summary:
Mastering vowel contrasts helps us speak more clearly and be understood better in English communication.

topics.title: Literature: drama analysis
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify themes in a drama, analyze character traits, and act out a scene to demonstrate understanding.

Introduction:
We have read stories and poems. Today we will analyze drama, which is written to be performed by actors.

Content:
Drama is literature written for performance on stage or screen. Theme is the main idea or message of the play. For example, in many Nigerian plays, the theme might be the conflict between tradition and modernity. Character analysis means understanding what motivates a character and how they change. A character might be brave like a warrior or wise like an elder. When we act a scene, we use our voices and bodies to show the characters' emotions and relationships. Nigerian plays often show characters dealing with issues like family expectations or community problems.

Class activity:
In small groups, choose a short scene from a Nigerian play. Analyze the theme and character traits, then perform the scene for the class.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between drama and other types of literature?
2. How would you describe the theme of a play about education in Nigeria?
3. What character traits can you identify from a character's actions?
4. Why is acting out a scene helpful for understanding drama?

Summary:
Drama analysis helps us understand the deeper messages and character relationships in plays written for performance.

topics.title: Summary writing
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify main ideas in a passage, write summaries in their own words, and reduce sentences to essential information.

Introduction:
When we read long passages, we need to remember the most important points. Today we will learn to write summaries.

Content:
A summary is a short version of a longer text that includes only the main ideas. To write a summary, first read the passage carefully. Identify the main points, usually in the first sentence of each paragraph. Leave out details, examples, and repetitions. Write the main points in your own words, not copying the original. For example, a passage about farming in Nigeria might have main points about types of crops, farming methods, and challenges. A good summary would be: "Nigerian farmers grow crops like yam and maize using traditional and modern methods, but face challenges like bad weather."

Class activity:
Read a passage about Nigerian festivals. Write a summary of 3-4 sentences, then compare with a partner to see if you captured the main ideas.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is a summary?
2. What should you leave out when writing a summary?
3. Why is it important to use your own words in a summary?
4. How long should a summary be compared to the original text?

Summary:
Summary writing helps us condense information and focus on the most important points from a longer passage.

topics.title: Revision and BECE practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to answer past BECE questions correctly, identify common mistakes, and improve their exam techniques.

Introduction:
We have covered many topics this term. Now we will practice with past BECE questions to prepare for the exam.

Content:
The BECE is an important exam for junior secondary students in Nigeria. Past questions help us understand the exam format and question types. When practicing, read each question carefully and understand what is being asked. Manage your time so you can answer all questions. For comprehension, read the passage before looking at the questions. For grammar questions, identify the grammar point being tested. For composition, plan your answer before writing. After answering, check for common mistakes like spelling errors or incomplete sentences.

Class activity:
Work in groups to answer a set of past BECE English questions. Discuss your answers and explain your reasoning to each other.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the purpose of practicing past BECE questions?
2. How should you approach comprehension questions in the exam?
3. What is the most common mistake students make in English exams?
4. How can you manage your time effectively during the BECE?

Summary:
Practicing with past questions helps us become familiar with the BECE format and improve our chances of success in the exam.
